entry.title: The 7 Very Best Cooling Mattress Toppers
entry.summary: To make your mattress more comfortable without making you sweat.
entry.content:
Adding a mattress topper is one of the easiest ways to change the feel of your mattress. However, if you tend to sleep warm, you’ll need one specifically designed to help you stay cool, so that solving one problem (making your bed more comfortable or supportive) won’t create another by causing you to overheat.

To curate this guide to the best cooling mattress toppers, I looked for toppers that incorporate cooling agents like gel, copper, or graphite infusions and that have covers made from breathable or cooling fabric or materials, including phase-change materials, which absorb heat to help regulate your body temperature. I took note of features that promote airflow, like perforations in a topper’s foam or mesh panels in its cover. I also included a latex foam topper, as latex typically stays cooler than memory foam, and an air-powered smart topper. The recommendations below include toppers tested and recommended by Strategist staffers as well as recommendations from sleep experts.

Updated on October 20, 2026
I added a note about two new “cooling sleep systems” that I tested this year, both of which use water to control the temperature of your bed. I also confirmed prices and availability for all the toppers on this list.

The filling of your mattress topper ultimately determines how cooling it can be. If you’re primarily looking for pressure relief and support, latex foam is my top choice for a cooling mattress topper because it offers a similar feel to memory foam but without as much heat retention (memory foam tends to absorb body heat and is often too dense to allow for much airflow). However, latex feels more springy and less sink-y than memory foam and doesn’t mold around the body as much. So if you are committed to the more contoured, enveloping feel of memory foam, you’ll want to choose a topper with gel, graphite, or another known cooling agent to help prevent you from overheating. The format of the fill is also important: Shredded or chopped foam will allow for more airflow than a solid slab.

Alternatively, a fiber mattress topper filled with cotton or polyester can add softness to a firm bed while counteracting the heat retention of a foam mattress. Each material has its pros and cons; having a clear idea of what you want from your mattress topper can help you decide on the best material for you. And while many brands tout the cooling benefits of their mattress toppers, Michael Grandner, director of the Sleep and Health Research Program at the University of Arizona, says to keep in mind that few scientific studies prove any one material or technology is superior for keeping cool.

Whether you’re shopping for mattress toppers, sheets, or pillows, you will inevitably encounter all kinds of promises about how a product will help to regulate your temperature. Cooling is more of an umbrella term that can refer to a variety of components, or even to how a mattress topper is assembled, so it can come from moisture-wicking materials like wool, bamboo, or Tencel; heat-absorbing or phase-change materials like gel, copper, or graphite; tangible features like ventilation holes; or a combination of all three. Some materials make a mattress topper feel cooler to the touch while others work to regulate your temperature as you sleep. Additionally, some tech-powered cooling toppers use water- or air-filled tubes throughout to offer precise temperature control. However, there aren’t many of these that actually alter the firmness or feel of the mattress, instead focusing solely on temperature control.

Mattress toppers range in thickness, usually between one and five inches. Thinner toppers, under two inches, will add less noticeable comfort, while thicker toppers, three inches and up, can totally transform the feel of a mattress.

It’s pretty common for mattress toppers to be returnable, so we have noted the length of the trial period and any warranty details for each topper below. But be sure to read the fine print: Companies that offer 100-night trials on mattresses don’t always offer the same terms on toppers, and return policies may vary depending on whether you buy the topper directly from the brand or from a third-party retailer like Amazon.

Cooling components: Copper-infused memory foam, phase-change material cover | Thickness: 4 inches | Trial and warranty: 90-day money-back guarantee, five-year warranty

Though memory foam has a reputation for trapping heat, this ViscoSoft topper stays surprisingly cool. I decided to test it after two experts recommended it, and was impressed with its cool-to-the-touch cover. And even after the initial burst of cooling faded, I never felt overheated. It’s infused with copper, a common cooling agent that can help draw heat away from the body, and its cover contains phase-change material, which, in my experience, is one of the most effective components to look for in a cooling sleep product. Phase-change material is something of a jargony term for encapsulated particles or fibers that literally change from solid to liquid depending on the surrounding temperature. “When you’re hot, the material liquifies” to absorb heat to keep you cool, and when you’re cool, “the material solidifies, trapping in the heat,” explains Joshua Tal, a psychologist specializing in sleep disorders.

The ViscoSoft Active Cooling topper is one of the thickest options on this list, at four inches tall. It is firmer than I expected it to be, and I didn’t sink too deeply into the foam, but it will still make a too-firm mattress feel more cushioned; it’s not so unyielding that I felt like I was floating on top of it, but also not so soft that I felt enveloped by it. It has a machine-washable cover, which I appreciate since memory foam is spot-clean only. The cover has adjustable straps on all four corners to keep the topper secured in place. With a nice balance between comfort and cooling, it’s my pick for the best cooling mattress topper overall.

Cooling components: Gel-infused foam, bamboo rayon cover | Thickness: Also available in 2 inches or 4 inches | Trial and warranty: 90-day money-back guarantee, five-year warranty

Also from ViscoSoft, the Select High Density topper is made with high-density, gel-infused foam, and it’s a good choice for a classic memory-foam feel with minimal heat retention. I like high-density foam because it’s usually very durable and supportive, thanks to its higher weight per cubic foot. The gel infusions are designed to help draw heat away from the body, similar to the copper infusions in the Active Cooling topper, above, and while the bamboo-rayon cover is not cool to the touch like the Active Cooling topper’s phase-change material cover, bamboo rayon is temperature-regulating and moisture-wicking. These differences in materials mean the Select High Density topper is significantly cheaper than the Active Cooling topper, while still offering meaningful temperature regulation. The Select High Density topper also still has corner straps to keep it from sliding around, which you don’t always see on lower-priced toppers.

When I tested this topper, the foam felt firm at first, but I sank in more deeply after lying on it for a few minutes; it contoured around me and provided excellent pressure relief. I especially liked how well it cushioned my shoulder, which sometimes jams up when I lie on my side, but the foam of this topper prevented any discomfort. As far as cooling goes, this topper didn’t feel overly chilly to the touch, but I didn’t feel it heating up around me excessively, which is sometimes all you can expect with memory foam. The bamboo cover and the gel infusions in the foam work together to keep the topper from overheating.

Strategist associate editor Jeremy Rellosa also likes the Select High Density topper — he’s been sleeping on it for about three years and says it’s very comfortable — but he does caution that the foam softens when it’s warm. “When my room is cold from AC, and when it’s cold outside, the topper is nice and firm. But when the weather is hot and humid, it can be so soft and soupy,” Rellosa explains. The change in firmness doesn’t affect the cooling properties, but can be an annoyance nonetheless. Rellosa says keeping the AC running can mostly prevent the softening — which many hot sleepers are likely to be doing anyway.

Overall, the Active Cooling topper is stronger in cooling than the Select High Density topper, as it has a noticeably cool-to-the-touch feel. But this one is a good option if you don’t want to spend $400 on a mattress topper, if you want thinner options, or if you want a slightly softer feel than the Active Cooling topper provides — though as Rellosa notes, it can get much softer depending on the weather.

Cooling components: Graphite-infused memory foam | Thickness: 3 inches | Trial and warranty: 180-day trial period, one-year limited warranty

Graphite is another common bedding material used to draw heat away from the body. This topper from Saatva — the maker of our favorite mattress — uses graphite-infused memory foam to create a plush but not too hot topper. When I tested it, I loved how thick and dense the foam felt. It contoured around my body with a nice balance of cushioning and support — I didn’t sink in quite as much as I did on the ViscoSoft High-Density topper. This one doesn’t feel cool to the touch, but it also didn’t feel noticeably hot. I like that on top of the graphite infusions, this topper has a breathable organic-cotton cover with straps to secure it in place on your mattress. However, I wish the cover were removable and washable instead of spot-clean only. On the plus side, Saatva offers a very generous 180-day trial period with this topper, so you have plenty of time to decide whether you like it.

Cooling components: Copper gel-infused memory foam | Thickness: 2 inches | Trial and warranty: 30-day trial period, five-year warranty

This two-inch topper from Layla features the same copper gel-infused foam used in Layla’s mattresses. Strategist writer Tembe Denton-Hurt sleeps on the Layla Hybrid mattress and says she and her partner never overheat.

While this topper is on the thinner side compared with others on this list, it has fairly dense foam, with a 2.5-pound density level. When I tested it, I sank into the foam quite slowly — it molded around my body the longer I lay on it, ultimately providing excellent pressure relief. As with the ViscoSoft High-Density topper, I felt hugged by this one, but the effect was lessened by the foam’s thinness (two inches versus three or four inches). Because the foam is dense in this topper, it will take a minute for your body to settle into it. Like the other toppers with infusions for cooling, the Layla topper didn’t feel noticeably cool, but I didn’t feel overheated.

Additionally, I like that this topper has a removable cover with straps, but Layla does recommend dry-cleaning the topper’s cover to maintain the softness, which is a little inconvenient.

Cooling components: Perforated latex | Thickness: 2 inches or 3 inches | Trial and warranty: 100-night sleep trial, 1-year warranty

Although generally more expensive than toppers made of memory foam or fiberfill, latex mattress toppers are great if you like a bouncier, more responsive feel and natural materials. They also tend to trap less heat than memory-foam toppers do. Avocado’s Eco Organic topper is made of perforated latex foam to allow for plenty of airflow and has a breathable organic-cotton cover. The topper comes in two thicknesses (two inches or three inches) and two firmnesses (medium or plush). Avocado makes its medium topper from Dunlop latex and its plush topper from Talalay latex; Dunlop tends to be firmer and denser, while Talalay tends to be softer and more pliant. Senior editor Jen Trolio has been sleeping on the three-inch plush Avocado Eco Organic topper for about four months and says it provides great pressure relief on her joints and lower back, like memory foam would, but doesn’t overheat. It doesn’t feel cool to the touch, but rather allows body heat to dissipate.

Cooling components: Polyethylene cooling cover | Thickness: 3.75 inches | Trial and warranty: 100-day trial, one-year limited warranty

If you’re looking for a topper that provides a little extra support — maybe to place atop a slightly sagging mattress — consider a micro-coil topper. These toppers, as the name suggests, have small coils in them to provide more structure and bounce, and which can also assist with airflow. This one from Helix is made with .75-inch coils sandwiched between two 1.5-inch sections of foam, like a mini hybrid mattress. The reason it earned a spot on this list is that it has a cooling cover made from Helix’s GlacioTex fabric, a 50-50 blend of polyester and polyethylene; polyethylene is a synthetic material that is commonly used in cooling products because it gives the fabric a slick and cool-to-the-touch feel that polyester alone doesn’t have. When I tried this topper, the cooling effect was most powerful when I was lying directly on the topper, but I could also still feel it through my sheets. I’ve tried one other micro-coil topper, from Saatva, which has much larger coils that add more bounce. The coils in this Helix topper aren’t nearly as noticeable, but I think they add more structured support to what could otherwise be three inches of pure foam, and the cover’s cooling abilities are on par with similar cooling toppers that I’ve tried. Just as importantly, the topper is really quite comfortable: It has enough foam to sink into to feel pressure relief, but the coils add enough extra oomph that it doesn’t become a total sinky-foam fest.

Cooling components: App-controlled fan cooling | Thickness: Approximately 2 inches | Trial and warranty: 30-day trial, one-year limited warranty

The Perfectly Snug Smart Topper is app-controlled and customizable so you can warm or cool it to your desired temperature. The topper has two main layers: a one-inch layer of memory foam and a one-inch layer of “3-D mesh,” the plastic layer the air actually flows through. Both of those layers are encased in a breathable mesh fabric. The topper has mini-fans at the corners or the foot of the topper, depending on which size you get, that blow warm or cool air through its surface. I tested a queen size, which had two fans — one in each corner at the foot of the bed. I didn’t notice them much, but they are covered with hard plastic that you could knock a foot against if your feet reach the end of the bed. When I set the temperature and lay down, I could feel that air was flowing underneath me, but I couldn’t feel distinct gusts or currents. The temperature change was obvious, but I never had the feeling of hot or cold air blowing directly on me (like you might feel in a car).

The Perfectly Snug is primarily controlled through an app, but it has physical-button controls on the side of the topper too. With the app, you choose a temperature setting between negative 10 and 10, as well as whether you want the temperature to change at all throughout the night or in the morning. The brand does not provide exact temperatures that correspond to each setting, so you’ll need to experiment a bit to find one that works for you. After sleeping on the topper for about two weeks, I landed on an ideal of between 1 and 3 for warming, or -1 and -3 for cooling. While the app feels a little outdated and isn’t especially intuitive to use, the topper itself is pretty effective. When I set it to a cool temperature, I could immediately feel air coming through the topper, which made for a much speedier temperature adjustment than I’ve felt with the water-powered cooling systems I’ve tested (more on those below). It’s worth noting, though, that the coolness of the cool air is dependent on the room temperature. The Perfectly Snug doesn’t work like air-conditioning to make the air colder; it just blows more air when you crank up the cooling. If the room is hot in the first place, the topper won’t do quite as much to cool you down. The heating option is powered by the same fans and works more like a forced-air space heater, which is nice for preheating your bed before hopping in. I also like that for a queen size and larger, each side of the topper can be set to different temperatures — ideal for partners who differ on their temperature preferences.

The Perfectly Snug is primarily designed for temperature control, but because it has a thin layer of memory foam, it will make your mattress feel slightly cushier. I tested it on our best-in-class mattress, the Saatva Classic, which is springy and somewhat firm, and I definitely felt more give with the Perfectly Snug topper than without. Still, it isn’t as plush or pressure-relieving as most of the other toppers on this list, so if adding softness is your highest priority, I’d go with a less techy topper.

The toppers I’ve included on this list alter the firmness and feel of your mattress by adding a layer of foam, latex, and/or springs, while preventing you from overheating with breathable or “cooling” materials (such as phase-change materials). But if you don’t care so much about changing the softness or firmness of your mattress and your goal is just to stay cool, a water-powered cooling system like the Eight Sleep Pod, Chilipad, or Orion can actively cool you a lot more than most regular toppers can. I’ve tested all three, which have cooling and heating capabilities and are extremely effective at regulating a mattress’s surface temperature; you can read my dedicated reviews of the Eight Sleep, Chilipad, and Orion for more details. I decided to leave them off this list of the best cooling mattress toppers, however, because none of them perform the primary function of a mattress topper; they are more akin to basic mattress pads that don’t provide any extra cushioning or support.

Another non-topper cooling system worth checking out is the BedJet 3 Climate Comfort, which is “basically a central-air unit under your covers,” as contributor Claire Zulkey put it in her BedJet review. While it is effective for cooling, I have also left the BedJet off the main list as it cools you by blowing air through your sheets, rather than changing the surface temperature of your mattress.

entry.title: The Strategist Guide to Shopping at Levi’s
entry.summary: Including a pair of jeans that has made just about every list of Strategist-approved jeans out there.
entry.content:
Anyone who has shopped at a bigger-box brand knows it can be hard to figure out where to begin. There are dozens of options that all seem as worthy as the next, but the reality is that not all products from any given brand are created equal. When you shop as regularly as we do, you learn that many brands just do some things better than they do other things. Levi’s, with more than 400 styles of jeans alone (in nearly as many washes), is one of those brands — its expansive inventory of denim, whether wide-leg, high-rise, or skinny-fit, must be carefully picked through to find the perfect pair. To make that task a little easier, we’ve sifted through our archives to put together a list of the Levi’s garments that celebrity stylists, denim experts, podcasters, plus-size models, stylish teens, and other cool people (including our writers and editors) have recommended on the Strategist.

Updated on July 29, 2026
We’ve made sure all of our top Levi’s picks are up to date with the latest stock and availability.

The Wedgie high-rise jeans have made just about every list of Strategist-approved jeans we have, from our master guide to jeans for women to our list of the very best high-waisted jeans. To put it simply: “It’s a cut that’s universally flattering and doesn’t go out of style,” writes Strategist denim correspondent Ambar Pardilla. Sara Zucker, director of social media at KORRES, says they have “a leg that’s slightly slimmer than your standard mom jean.” “They’re popular because they fit you like you want old 501s to fit,” explains Bird clothing founder Jennifer Mankins: A “perfect straight leg, but with a bit more of a generous, modern cut.” She describes the rise as “high, but not too high,” and the jeans have a subtle stretch — never more than one percent elastane — which makes them “a bridge between too-rigid and too-stretchy denim” in Pardilla’s eyes. They’re available in multiple inseam lengths (26, 28, and 30 inches) and nearly a dozen washes, so you can choose a pair that fits your height and color preferences.

Compared to, say, some regular Wedgies, Levi’s shaping jeans have a higher percentage of polyester, LYCRA, and viscose, which gives the jeans more stretch. In particular, the 315 Shaping Bootcut Jeans are another favorite among plus-size women, so much so that we’ve named the pair the “best plus-size boot-cut jeans.” Its fans include model Yasmin Geurts, who calls the style her “everyday go-to for work.” She says they “come in right at my belly button and suck in everything,” adding that the flared legs “actually balance all my curves.” Geurts also loves the jeans’ wider back pockets, telling us they make her butt “look great” because of the way the pockets “fan out to the side a little.”

The wide leg shaping jeans are a favorite of producer Mbiye Kasonga. In fact, they’re the jeans that got her back into denim. And while the polyester and LYCRA make the jeans more stretchy, she notes there’s still a waist gap — “though it’s not prohibitive to wearing them.”

Levi’s Ribcage Ankle jeans — the “Goldilocks of jeans,” as we like to call them — are beloved by New York deputy editor Alexis Swerdloff as well as by former Strategist editor Maxine Builder, who describes the rise as “deliriously high, easily clearing my belly button,” but promises that they don’t “feel uncomfortable when I sit.” Swerdloff agrees, describing them as “stiff without being too constricting” and having “just the right amount of flare.” The jeans have appeared in just about every guide to women’s jeans on our site as our favorite super-high-waisted pair. “The jeans don’t cut into your ribcage, as their name would suggest,” clarifies Pardilla. “Instead, they simply cinch you at the waist.” Like the Wedgies, these are available in nearly a dozen colors and three different inseams, which means they are ideal for tall and short women alike. Content creator Amy Serrano, who is five feet tall, counts them as one of her favorite pairs, saying, “This pair gives me legs for days because of the ultrahigh waist. It hugs what it needs to hug, and the rest of the leg is a nice relaxed straight fit.”

This classic cut counts multiple fashionable people among its fans, including Queer Eye star Tan France, musicians Aly and AJ Michalka, and celebrity stylist Karla Welch (who has collaborated with Levi’s on capsule collections). “I’ve been wearing this style of Levi’s since I was 12 years old, when I stole a pair from my brother, which I still have,” Welch told us, adding that, like many pairs on this list, these relaxed-fit jeans only get better with wear and age. France used to wear men’s 501s but prefers these because they have “a little bit of a higher waist — I love a high waist — and tapered fit.” And Aly calls them “just classic: the fit, the semi-high waist, the color. I probably own six or seven pairs.” It’s worth noting that you won’t find any stretch here. In fact, Welch used to sit in a bathtub with the jeans on to get them to fit as a teen. Like any jeans that get better with time, there’s only one solution: “Wearing them and wearing them and wearing them and wearing them,” she says.

Until she realized she could simply buy cropped Levi’s, Strategist senior writer Lauren Ro could never find straight leg jeans that worked with her five-foot-two-frame and curvy hips and thighs. Since adding the 501 Cropped Originals — which have a high-ish rise, a classic straight-leg cut that’s fitted through the hip and thigh, and two inseam options, 26-inch and 28-inch — they’ve become her “throw-them-on-for-whatever-situation jeans.”

A slouchier and low-slung version of the Levi’s 501s, the 501 ’90s are petite-friendly, too. “They are the perfect ‘baggy’ length — so not too long they touch the floor but long enough that you get that cool ’90s vibe,” says Andrea Ventura, petite-model coach and founder of the podcast Standing Tall. Unlike the Ribcages, which sit high above the belly button, these sit about an inch below hers, making them “incredibly comfortable” and possible to be cool-teen-approved, too.

Former Strategist senior editor Casey Lewis owns the shorts version of Levi’s 501 women’s jeans, naming them a great alternative to a full-length pair when working from home. “Although I was tempted by the Ribcage and Wedgie fits, I ultimately went with the classic (and less constricting) 501s,” says Lewis, who got hers in a size up so that they’d be “extra comfy.” (She also bought the longer knee-length version so she could further cut them herself.) Strategist contributor Maria Dueñas Jacobs, the founder of kids’ jewelry brand Super Smalls, has also recommended 501 shorts (though she prefers buying them vintage rather than new): “Like jeans, I can never get enough.”

The Plus-Size Wedgie jeans are a favorite of model Felicity Hayward, who told us that they are unbeatable when it comes to style and quality. She describes the sizing in one word — “perfect” — and adds that the jeans “can be paired with sneakers for a more casual look, or with some pointed stilettos to elongate those lovely legs.”

Compared to the Wedgies or Ribcages, these jeans are wider at the leg and loose through the hips and thighs. There’s no stretch in them, but writer Jo Rosenthal, who’s a fan of the style, says the jeans have “that Levi’s worn-in” feel from the beginning. Brand consultant Katie Stone, another fan, agrees: “They feel like home to me,” she says. “I don’t even consider having them on as ‘wearing jeans’; they’re in a different category of their own.” Just note, of the three pairs she owns, she says the darker washes “fit a bit tighter around the butt and hold their shape better” than the lighter ones.

We’ve billed these “low-rise jeans for low-rise skeptics” since they can fit as either low-rise or mid-rise jeans depending on which size and wash you get. (Some washes have a higher percentage of elastane that makes it possible to pull them up whenever you’d rather have a mid-rise fit. That said, if you prefer a more rigid denim, be sure to look at the fabric composition before checking out.) Its fans include cool teens, Mya Gelber, and our junior writer Bella Druckman, who says they’re flattering on the behind unlike most low-rise jeans.

“Even as their merits have been contested, I still think skinny jeans are worth having in your closet,” says Pardilla. So, if you’re looking for that one pair, try these. According to writer Diana McCorry, Levi’s 720 High Rise Super Skinny jeans strike a very happy medium: They have enough stretch “to avoid that nasty tummy compression” but enough shape to “create a great silhouette when you stand up.” They’re also good for those who often have problems with waist gaps, as McCorry finds these jeans to be only “a little loose in the waist, but not quite enough to necessitate a belt.”

Given how many times we’ve featured Levi’s in our jeans guides, it’s no surprise that it makes our favorite jean jacket, too. “After just a few wears, it was obvious to me that the ’90s Trucker jacket is everything I want in a jean jacket: It’s a mix of sturdy and slouchy with a mid-weight feel that’s ideal for every season — and it’s under $100,” says Strategist junior writer Brenley Goertzen. That sturdy-yet-slouchy look comes from the jacket’s fabric composition — 79 percent cotton and 21 percent Tencel — a big difference from the more rigid 100 percent cotton pieces that you need to wear and wear and wear to stretch out. “The blended fabric makes it super-wearable and gives it a nice lived-in feel, like a jean jacket you might have thrifted,” Goertzen adds.

While it might be a tie between the Wedgies, the Ribcages, and the 501s for women, there’s no doubt that the 501s are the favorite Levi’s jeans among the guys we’ve interviewed about jeans. They’ve garnered praise from denim experts, writers, podcasters, and Strategist columnist Chris Black alike. “If we’re going to talk about jeans that every man should have in their closet, a pair of good-old Levi’s” is a must, according to denim expert and writer Amy Leverton, who calls 501s the gold standard of men’s denim. Former Strategist writer David Notis is also a fan, calling out the jeans’ “strong hardware and 100 percent cotton” material, which he says is non-stretch and therefore tends to hold its shape better as the jeans age. Jeremy Kirkland, the host of men’s style podcast Blamo!, swears by 501s, too, because their high rise makes them easier to dress up. “I’ve always been a fan of higher-rise jeans versus the lower-rise pairs because I wear tailoring and sport coats, so it helps to wear something totally high,” he says.

Levi’s 501s may forever hold a spot in the jeans Hall of Fame, but Strategist senior writer Michael Zhao could never find a pair that fit “bubble butt just as well as my spindly legs.” That is until the brand released the Levi’s 501 loose jeans, which have a higher rise and a loose fit through the thigh and leg. The size 30, specifically, has a 12.5-inch rise that matches how these pants fit back in the 1980s, which “helps the waistband sit more comfortably at my natural waist and creates a more flattering, leg-extending silhouette that pairs well with a boxy tee,” he says.

As Noah Rinsky, creator of Old Jewish Men, tells us in our “59 Tasteful People on the Best Jeans They Own” guide, “I have a big tuchus and chicken legs.” As such, he prefers loose-fitting jeans like Levi’s 550s. “They’re loose on the thighs with generous pockets for my large Temu wallet, a smooth zipper for easy access, and a deep-blue denim that hides stains,” he says. “What more can a guy who spills his coffee a lot ask for?”

“Skinny but not skintight” is how Netflix brand and editorial manager Alex Simons describes the fit of these jeans. He promises that they’re “comfortable from the moment you put them on” and that they have the “perfect amount of pocket space.” Simmons adds that he was a “fancy-jeans guy for years,” opting for pricier pairs from brands like Marc by Marc Jacobs until he tried these on and, as he puts it, “never looked back.”

The Levi’s 511 is to slim-fit jeans as the 501 is to straight-leg jeans: a standard-bearer. Menswear writer Tim Melideo told us that 511s are a staple in his wardrobe, and stylist Brandon Garr likes them, too — especially their price, which he says allows him to “be a little bit more daring in them because I don’t have to worry as much about the replacement cost if they get a little roughed up.” And chef Jacques Torres appreciates that these “give a little bit, so if I gain a couple of pounds, I don’t have to change my jeans.” He compares bad jeans to bad knives: “If you feel like your jeans are a prison and you don’t feel good in them, then you should change your jeans. There is no reason to wear bad jeans, just like there is no reason to put up with a bad knife,” he advises.

entry.title: The Best Lawn Mowers, According to Landscaping Professionals
entry.summary: Grass choppers that get the job done effectively and efficiently every time.
entry.content:
Whether you’re trimming a small urban lawn or maintaining a sprawling suburban property, a battery-powered walk-behind mower makes cutting grass easier without the noise, fumes, or upkeep of a gas model. If you worry that cordless mowers lack the muscle for thick grass or the run time to finish the job, it’s time to reconsider. Today’s models deliver plenty of power for weekly cuts and enough battery life to finish on a single charge. Battery-powered models can cost more upfront than gas mowers, but some reports suggest they can pay for themselves in about two years through savings on fuel and maintenance. During that time, you can skip oil changes, winter fuel drainage, air filters, and spark plugs, though you’ll still need to sharpen the blade and (depending on where you live) store batteries indoors out of season to protect them from extreme temperatures.

Professional landscapers need equipment that matches the performance of gas-powered gear without running into battery-life problems, and they’re increasingly turning to battery-powered mowers. “We put mowers through years of testing,” says Dan Mabe, founder of American Green Zone Alliance, which tests battery-powered lawn mowers. “We place them in the hands of professionals to amass hours on them, and we also give them to residential users and verify manufacturers’ run-time claims.” George Carrette, owner of EcoQuiet Lawn Care in Concord, Massachusetts, has used battery-powered equipment for years. He thinks homeowners might be surprised by today’s mowers’ power and battery capacity but cautions against taking manufacturers’ run-time claims at face value. “If you’re mowing weekly, then the stated run time could be realistic, but if you mow every other week and the grass is wet, the run time could easily be half of what’s stated,” he says. Carrette found that keeping the blade sharp — even if that means taking a file or grinder to it more frequently than you would with a gas mower — also maximizes the run time and gives you a better cut quality.

Is it time for you to switch to a battery-powered lawn mower? We asked landscapers, experts, and homeowners who’ve spent hours cutting lawns which models they recommend for your yard.

You’ll find push mowers powered by batteries from 18 volts to 82 volts, but our experts recommend choosing a higher-voltage platform. If you’re switching from a gas-powered walk-behind with a 20- or 22-inch-wide blade and you were happy with how long it took to mow your lawn with that machine, chances are a battery-powered equivalent needs at least a 36-volt battery.

That voltage doesn’t have to come from a single battery. While we recommend some models that use single 40-, 56-, and 80-volt batteries, some mowers use two 18-volt units that drain simultaneously, delivering the cutting power and torque of a 36-volt model (and those models will usually only work if both batteries have at least some charge).

Walk-behind mower kits can include batteries in the four to 12 amp hour (Ah) range. Of all the battery-powered lawn and garden gear, mowers tend to come packaged with the heaviest and most expensive batteries because you need the run time and users are not carrying the weight around as they would be with a hedge trimmer, leaf blower, or string trimmer. In a pinch, you can use a string trimmer’s 4Ah battery in your mower for a few extra minutes of run time, but you might not want to use a mower’s battery in your trimmer. Mowers ship with higher-capacity batteries that can weigh a pound or two more, making them less practical for one-handed tools like leaf blowers.

Before choosing a battery-powered mower, consider what else its batteries can power. If you already own some outdoor tools, look at the mowers your favorite brand has available. Mowers are often sold as kits because they need larger, higher-capacity batteries than most other yard tools, so they’re often sold with larger packs or multiple smaller batteries. If you’re starting from scratch, look at the brand’s broader lineup of equipment: Ego, Stihl, and Greenworks focus on outdoor tools, while Ryobi, Milwaukee, and DeWalt offer batteries that work across a wider range of shop and outdoor equipment.

A mower’s cutting width — the strip of grass it clears in one pass — is slightly narrower than its deck width, which is the mower’s physical width. Deck width matters when you’re planning storage or checking whether the mower will fit through a gate. Smaller models are typically 16 to 18 inches wide, mid-size models are 20 to 22 inches, and wide-area walk-behinds are usually 30 inches or wider. If you’re happy with how long your current mower takes to finish the lawn, stick with a similar cutting width. However, if mowing takes close to an hour — which is the max most homeowners want to be at it — consider a wider model. But before stepping up to a wide-area walk-behind, which uses two blades side-by-side, check that it can fit through any gates between your front and back yards.

Many manufacturers offer push and self-propelled versions of their mowers, with the latter versions more expensive (the feature adds $100 or more to the price). The range of speed is usually from 1 to 4 miles per hour, though most users walk at somewhere between 2 and 2.5. On hills or a larger yard, self-propulsion can make mowing less tiring and easier to control. It can also help you move the mower to and from storage, though you’ll still need both hands to steer and manage the controls. On a small, flat lawn, you may not need the extra assistance. Self-propulsion also uses battery power, reducing run time, though you can usually turn it off.

Most mowers offer six or seven cutting-height settings, typically ranging from about one to four inches. Adjustment styles vary: a single lever moves all four wheels at once for maximum convenience, while two-lever systems take extra effort. Models with a separate adjustment at each wheel are the slowest to change.

Steel decks resist impacts better than plastic, but they add weight, cost, and can rust if scratched. Plastic or composite decks will not rust, are lighter, and can be shaped to improve airflow, but they can crack under severe impact. A lighter deck can make the mower easier to maneuver and may help preserve battery run time, especially with self-propel engaged. Pros favor the durability of steel, but for a homeowner it can be less important — unless you have a teenager mowing your lawn.

Most mowers today offer three cutting options: mulching, side discharge, and bagging. Since these features are common, they rarely determine which mower you buy. Still, check that the box includes the parts needed for all three.

Some manufacturers offer mowers with two stacked blades, which can cut grass into finer clippings that blend into the lawn when you mulch. The extra blade increases the purchase price by roughly $150, reduces run time, and requires maintaining two non-interchangeable parts. If you usually bag clippings, you may not need this feature, but if you mulch, the finer clippings can leave a neater-looking lawn behind.

Cutting width: 21 inches | Volts: 56 | Included battery: 7.5 Amp-hours | Run time with included battery: up to 60 minutes | Recharge time: About 45 minutes | Self-propelled? Yes

The LM2125SP is part of Ego’s entry-level 600 series, and while you can spend nearly $300 more on the manufacturer’s most premium single-blade, 21-inch mower, this one does not skimp on any important features or performance. In fact, after testing with professional crews and homeowners, the American Green Zone Alliance (AGZA) certified the LM2125SP, finding it stood up to heavy-duty use and delivered cut quality that competes with gas models.

Ego covers the composite deck and mower with a five-year warranty, while backing the 7.5-Ah battery for three years. That power pack delivers about an hour of run time, which is about as long as most users want to be mowing, but it’s also a very useful size to work across Ego’s other 56-volt tools that need a longer run time, like a snow blower, pressure washer, or inverter.

The mower has up to 6.0 foot-pounds of torque — the force required to sever thick, tall, or wet grass. It’s common to see gas walk-behind mowers with 5.5 to 7.5 foot-pounds of torque. The Ego’s seven cutting heights are adjustable with one lever, and handlebars that slide in and out to fit users of different heights. “Touch Drive” means that the self-propelled motor is controlled by a wheel mounted on the handlebar, which is intuitive to swipe up or down with a thumb. Levers (conveniently styled in a bright green) also make the mower’s folding mechanism easy to use. If you need more run time, a second 4Ah battery can add about 30 minutes.

Cutting width: 18 inches | Volts: 36 | Included battery: 5 Amp-hours | Run time with included battery: up to 47 minutes | Recharge time: About 60 minutes | Self-propelled? No

“The Stihl RMA 348 is a good, entry-level mower for the average homeowner with a smaller yard,” says Curtis Atkinson, of Sunshine Landscapes in Bluffdale, Utah. “It’s got plenty of run time for a small- to medium-sized lawn, and the batteries are known for consistency, so the power won’t drop off as the battery discharges.”

The RMA 348 feels easy to use, with a soft-grip handle, push-button start, and a single lever that quickly sets the cutting height to seven positions. When grass gets taller or tougher, the boost button adds power to help you keep moving. Like all Stihls, it’s backed by just about the strongest warranty in outdoor power equipment. If you like the idea of a small mower, but want self-propelled, Stihl offers that feature in the RMA 348 V, which typically costs about $150 more, but is a great deal if you can find on sale, whe it’s priced at just around $50 more than the standard RMA 348.

Cutting width: 21 inches | Volts: 80 | Included battery: 4 Amp-hours: | Run time with included battery: up to 33 minutes | Run time with included battery: About 40 minutes | Self-propelled? Yes

This 80-volt Greenworks offers more power than its competitors: enough to avoid stalling in thicker turf like zoysia and St. Augustine grass. It’s available with a larger 8Ah battery, but the standard 4Ah version is enough for Jon Graham of Element Plumbing, Heating, Air & Electrical in St. George, Utah, to mow his sizable front yard. “I focus on run time and on our larger, 4,000-square-foot lawn, I’m getting closer to 35 or 40 minutes before I swap to a second battery,” he says. The self-propelled drive also makes mowing a mostly one-handed task.

The mower has seven cutting-height settings and a dashboard that shows the charge level of the battery. The battery’s recharge time with the included charger is nearly equal to its run time, so a second battery can be charging while you mow with the first-a practical setup for tackling a larger lawn.

Cutting width: 21 inches | Volts: 60 | Included battery: 5 Amp-hours | Run time with included battery: up to 45 minutes | Recharge time: About 50 minutes | Self-propelled? No

Romkee likes this Greenworks mower because its battery works with other lawn and garden tools, and it can make quick work of the lawn, especially if you have two batteries. Like many mowers, it offers bagging, mulching, and side discharge, but it also has a turbo button that spins the blade up to 3,200 RPM — slightly faster than the roughly 3,000 RPM maximum on many models. With the bag attached, that mode creates suction that can pull up dry leaves, mulch them, and send them to the bag, helping cut down on raking.

The mower has a sturdy steel deck and a single lever with seven cutting-height settings, from 1.3 to four inches. Its dual battery ports let you carry a second battery to extend run time; the mower automatically switches to the second battery when the first runs out. Plus, the handle can be adjusted to accommodate users of different heights, and folds down for compact storage.

Cutting width: 20.1 inches | Volts: 36 | Included battery: 7.2 Amp-hours | Run time with included battery: about 50 minutes | Recharge time: About 80 minutes | Self-propelled? Yes

“The mower is exceptionally quiet and provides a beautiful cut,” says Jacob Romkee of Vintage Lawn Service and a member of Thumbtack’s Pro Advisory Board, who also appreciates the RMA 510 V’s compatibility with Stihl’s wide lineup of tools. “These mowers can fit their smaller batteries, the AP 300s and AP 500s, which can fit directly into their weed trimmers, hedge trimmers, as well as some of their blowers,” And Stihl backs the battery (and mower) with an industry-leading five-year warranty, whereas most brands offer three.

The Stihl has a 21-inch steel deck, but its smooth, ball-bearing wheels make it feel lighter and easier to maneuver than similar, full-size mowers. It has room for two batteries, but the second bay is just for convenience and extended run time; it uses one at a time. By the way, it doesn’t switch to the second one automatically — you’ll need to swap them yourself. Eco mode adjusts the motor’s output to match the cutting conditions, to power through tall or thick grass, and help conserve battery power. Height adjustment is with a single lever to set all four wheels, and you get eight cutting heights, from under one inch to about four inches.

Cutting width: 20 inches | Volts: 18 | Included battery: 6 Amp-hours: | Run time with included battery: Up to 40 minutes | Recharge time: About 3 hours | Self-propelled? Yes

These days, for an 18-volt mower to compete on all but the smallest lawns, it needs teamwork. The two 18 volt batteries in the Ryobi work in concert to provide 36 volts, giving you gas-like cut quality and power. For homeowners with a long list of indoor and outdoor tasks, Ryobi might be the most accommodating platform out there with more than 300 tools that use the batteries that come with this mower. While a 6Ah battery, and its nearly 2-pound weight, might not be comfortable strapped to a drill/driver, you’ll appreciate the punchy run time on something like a leaf blower, utility vacuum, power station, and lighting.

On the lawn, the Ryobi PBLLM05K2 is a capable gas alternative, with a motor that automatically adjusts blade speed according to the load to handle tougher grass and self-propelled rear-wheel drive for easier mowing. Its main drawback is the basic, slow charger: a depleted battery takes about three hours to recharge, even though the kit includes two chargers. A faster charger would be a smart investment to reduce downtime between mowing sessions.

Cutting width: 42 inches | Volts: 80 | Included battery: 6 Amp-hours: | Run time with included battery: Up to 90 minutes | Recharge time: About 3.5 hours | Self-propelled? Yes

If your lawn is larger than 3/4 of an acre or takes more than an hour to mow — especially if it has few trees or garden beds to maneuver around and no steep hills — it may be time to consider a riding mower. “The 80-volt riding mowers would work great for many homeowners,” says contractor and interior designer Eric Goranson. “Everyone I’ve met likes them,” says George Carrette, who uses a Greenworks walk-behind mower on the job as owner, and als uses the company’s 80 volt riding mower.

The 42-inch 12-gauge steel deck adjusts from 1.5 to 4.5 inches across seven positions with a single lever reachable right from the seat, and the ride-on can clear between 1.5 and 2 acres on a single charge. It tops out at an 8 MPH transport speed, to get it back and forth from the garage, and mows at a brisk 5 MPH cutting speed while handling slopes up to 15 degrees (Carrette notes that, “they can be a bit tricky on hills”). While small, the rear cargo bed holds up to 200 pounds for bags of mulch, soil, or firewood. Equipped with a standard two-inch rear hitch, it can tow pull-behind attachments weighing up to 350 pounds. Like an EV, the Greenworks has a charging port for its included wall-mounted charger. You can also remove the batteries to power other Greenworks lawn and garden tools, or even lifestyle gear including an e-bike.

entry.title: My Predictions for the Best Beauty Advent Calendars of the Year
entry.summary: Including Liberty London, Lush, and Jo Malone.
entry.content:
As we reported last week, Advent calendars have already started to arrive. Usually they land in early-to-mid-October, but this year the timeline has been pushed up to mid-September, similar to how the good Halloween decorations now pop up in July. The Liberty Advent calendar is already live, as is the Anthropologie one, both of which tend to sell out long before Christmas. Lots of the other calendars go on sale after September 15, and I expect those will go quickly too. As always, the deals vary. Some of the calendars contain lots of full-size products, while others have an assortment of travel and mini sizes for a wide range of brands. Like last year, I’ll be updating this often and making note as new calendars launch or sell out.

The Liberty London Advent calendar essentially invented the category. It was a big hit when it was released in 2014, prompting other department stores, and eventually brands, to launch their own. Every year, the brand tries to one-up itself; this year, there are 29 products, 21 of which are full size and valued at over $1,700, which Liberty says is its highest yet. The haul this year is pretty good. There are a couple fragrances, including the beloved Escentric Molecules Molecule 01, a facial oil from Augustinus Bader, and the Miracle Balm from Jones Road, an allover product that has amassed a following among beautyheads.

In recent years, Liberty has also introduced a men’s calendar. The 2026 calendar has fewer full-size products — 14 instead of 21 — but still contains some exciting stuff like a very fancy lip balm from La Mer, a hyaluronic acid serum from Paula’s Choice, and Loewe cologne.

Of all the calendars, Dermstore’s is my favorite. The curation is always solid and it contains a good mix of full-size and deluxe samples. Some of the products from this year I’m excited about: a full size of the iS Clinical wrinkle serum, a favorite of stylist Karla Welch; the BioEffect EGF Serum, which we’ve previously recommended for mature skin; and the Paula’s Choice niacinamide serum, which helps to even out and brighten skin.

Bloomingdale’s also has a good calendar this year. It features 25 days of products across a range of brands and categories, including a hair clip from Emi Jay, a candle from Jo Malone, travel-size fragrances from Maison Francis Kurkdjian and Le Labo, and a full-size lotion from La Mer.

If fragrance is more your speed, Bloomingdale’s also has a scent-focused advent calendar housed in a box reminiscent of a Venus et Fleur bouquet. There’s something in there for every nose: a Delina-scented Parfum de Marly body cream, a favorite of Real Housewives star Phaedra Parks; a fresh, woody scent from Jo Malone; and Byredo Gypsy Water, Christina Ricci’s go-to fragrance from the last decade.

The Anthropologie Advent calendar is massively popular — it’s often one of the first to sell out. It’s also one of the best. This year’s is packed with Strategist-approved products including Verb Ghost Oil, Supergoop Play lotion, Vacation’s nice-smelling sunscreen oil, and Salt & Stone’s deodorant.

For a less-expensive option, Anthropologie also makes a 12-day version that’s half the price. This one has an entirely different selection of products, so you could double up if you wanted. It’s currently available for preorder and starts shipping around October 22.

The Revolve calendar always sells out, which I suspect is because it offers impressive value for the money. It contains 27 products, almost half of which are full size, and is a mix of popular products and newer, emerging brands. Some highlights: Verb shampoo and conditioner, a mini Foreo UFO toning device, Ouai detox shampoo, and Supergoop sunscreen.

Laneige is also offering a 12-day calendar this year. It’s filled with minis of popular products like the beloved lip sleeping mask, the glowy lip balm, and a few products from the iconic Water Bank line.

Burt’s Bees chapstick fans, rejoice! This calendar contains 12 days of lip balms in an assortment of flavors, including seasonal scents like sugar cookie and cranberry spritz.

Typology releases a substantial advent calendar every year valued at around double the price. This year, the brand is offering something for every part of your routine, including a full size of writer Arielle Avila’s favorite vitamin-C serum, which layers well under moisturizers and helps to fade her acne scars.

The M.A.C advent calendar is a nice mix of full-size and mini beauty products and includes iconic products like M.A.C Ruby Woo, a beauty staple; lip liner in Whirl, a classic pink; and a tube of Lipglass, one of my favorite glosses of all time.

This year’s Free People advent calendar was curated with your beauty ritual in mind. It’s a mix of essentials like SPF from Vacation and deodorant from Salt & Stone, both products we’ve written about before. The price point is also decent for what you’re getting: 24 deluxe and travel-size products from popular brands.

Bloomingdale’s has partnered with Alice + Olivia founder Stacey Bendet on a seven-day beauty advent calendar comprised of her favorite products, like a 111Skin face mask and a YSL lip gloss. There’s also two Alice + Olivia branded products — a Touchland hand-sanitizer case and a lip-gloss charm.

Sephora Collection has two advent calendars this season, standard and premium. The premium one offers 24 days of surprises, most of which are full size, and comes in a sequined case.

I like this Conair calendar for tweens — it’s 12 days of hair accessories, ranging from cherry hair clips to curled scrunchies.

A mix of Lush’s greatest hits, the 25-day Advent calendar is a nice assortment of the brand’s offerings. There’s a hair primer, scented candle, body lotion, and lots of bath bombs, which will take care of your bath routine for the month and beyond. Most years, the Advent calendar comes in a decorative box, but this year’s comes in a handwoven Grinch-green basket that can be used after the gifts run out.

If the most exciting part of Lush’s Advent calendar is the bath bombs, this one might be more appealing. It contains 25 fizzy bath bombs and is slightly cheaper than the bigger calendar. It is also available for preorder but ships a bit earlier, starting on September 14.

We’ve written about the Elemis cleansing balm a bunch. It gently removes makeup and SPF — actress Abby Elliott even uses it to take off the false lashes she wears on set. Get a full size of the balm in this calendar, along with 24 other Elemis products.

L’Occitane has a few Advent calendars at different retailers this season, but I’m most excited about the premium one on its website. It contains a full-size shower oil (a staple in my shower routine), an assortment of hand creams in the brand’s popular scent, and a suite of body products in travel sizes so you can test them out.

This year’s Jo Malone Advent calendar comes in a gift-worthy trunk, with each surprise wrapped in plaid. There are 24 days of minis, ranging from travel-size candles to hand creams, and culminates in a full-size cologne on the 25th.

The Charlotte Tilbury Advent calendar regularly sells out by Christmas, and this year it may go even faster. For the first time, it contains two accessories: a makeup bag and a gua sha, compelling additions for fans of the brand.

For a discerning nose, Aesop has released a 13-day calendar with travel sizes of products like the cult-favorite hand cream and bar soap. There’s also a few things for the home, like a room spray in the scent Olous, which has notes of grapefruit, jasmine, and galbanium, and a Ptolemy Aromatique candle. It isn’t quite out yet, but you can sign up for the waiting list and be notified when it goes on sale.

Maison Louis Marie makes some of my favorite affordable fragrances; the scent No. 04 has been a staple in my perfume wardrobe for years. The 12-day advent calendar is a good opportunity to try a cross section of the brand’s offerings — there’s hand creams, travel sprays, a room spray, and even a deodorant.

At $525, this is one of the pricier advent calendars on the list, but I think it’s worth the price, given that it contains six fragrances and nine mini-candles, including Baies, a celebrity favorite.

entry.title: You Don’t Have to Wear a Plastic Fleece This Fall
entry.summary: Even Patagonia is now selling quarter-zips made from warm yet breathable wool.
entry.content:
Introduced in the early 1980s by Patagonia, synthetic polar fleece was intended as a cheaper, more lightweight, and more durable alternative to wool. And it really caught on. Easier to wash, quicker to dry, and less susceptible to moths than the knit sweaters of yore, fleece proved ideal for making cozy, outdoor-friendly clothing that also worked as streetwear. When Patagonia transitioned into using recycled materials in the 1990s, its fleeces came to be regarded as a futuristic and even ecofriendly wardrobe staple.

We now think of them differently. Research has shown that synthetic fleece sheds higher amounts of non-biodegradable microplastic fibers into waterways than other synthetic materials when laundered, and a growing number of studies even suggest that exercising in polyester clothing may pose personal health risks due to plastic exposure. As consumer awareness around these issues grows, brands have responded by designing lower-shed synthetic fabrics, or else manufacturing fleeces from the very natural fibers they once rebelled against. This season, you can buy a wool (or at least wool-blend) fleece from L.L.Bean, J.Crew, and even Patagonia itself.

Thanks to developments in textile science, the new breed of wool fleeces look and feel very similar to the polyester ones we’ve all been wearing for decades. They’re soft and textured rather than coarse and itchy. You can even toss them in the wash, although it’s still best to avoid hot tumble dryers.

Over the past few months, I’ve been trying out natural-fiber fleeces from a number of brands, from New Zealand–based Icebreaker (which, alongside sister brand Smartwool, also owned by VF, has helped pioneer and popularize technical fabrics made from merino and small percentages of nylon) to Portland-based Gnuhr (a trendy ultralight hiking upstart with streetwear roots). Some were made from 100 percent wool, whereas others were woven with a small percentage of polyester, elastane, nylon, or Tencel (a man-made, tree-derived fiber that’s part of the rayon family of materials) for added durability as well as stretch for athletic use.

Aside from wool being more expensive than polyester, it was an easy switch to make; I genuinely prefer to sweat it out while wearing breathable natural fibers rather than clammy plastic ones. They are not, in my experience, all that more fussy to wash or dry compared to polyester fleeces. And you don’t need to do so as frequently, because they’re naturally odor resistant. I tend to hang-dry anyway, in order to save energy and extend the life of my clothes.

As for their environmental and personal health benefits, it depends on who you talk to. If a wool garment is labeled as machine washable, that likely means it has been treated with the synthetic resin Hercosett, which increases shrink resistance but is technically (you guessed it!) a plastic. The environmental threat posed by any single polyester fleece might be overstated, anyway. Studies suggest that the majority of them appear to stop shedding large quantities of microplastic fibers after their first five laundry cycles, so there’s no need to panic too much about the five-year-old Patagonia Synchilla hanging in your closet right now. (In recent years, Patagonia has also developed synthetic fleece options that resist pilling and supposedly shed fewer microplastic fibers.)

Because of its fluffy weave, fleece fabric will always shed, whatever it’s made from — the ocean is full of cotton, silk, and wool microthreads as well as plastic ones. Happily, a recent peer-reviewed study indicates that these natural fibers are likely biodegradable in ocean water, even when they’ve been treated with synthetics for increased durability.

If you are in the market for a new fleece this fall, know that you’ve suddenly got plenty of attractive non-plastic options as well as the classic polyester ones. Either way, if you’re a fan of fuzzy clothing, I suggest purchasing a fiber-catching washing-machine filter or laundry bag.
